newsitem.title: UK: UBS analyst sees 3 bln stg tax hikes in UK budget.
newsitem.headline: UBS analyst sees 3 bln stg tax hikes in UK budget.

text.p: Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS in London, said he expects the Labour government to tighten fiscal policy by around three billion stg in its first budget on July 2.

In his budget analysis, he said Labour's commitment to stick to public spending plans laid down by the previous Conservative government meant any tightening had to come from the revenue side of the equation.
There was a significant risk that it might be directed towards the corporate sector, including a removal of the dividend tax credit to tax-exempt institutions, rather than the personal sector.

"Under this scenario, consumers' expenditure is likely to be much stronger for longer and the Bank of England is likely to tighten monetary policy more aggressively than we have assumed in our economic forecasts," Cates wrote.

"If the burden of taxation on the personal sector is not raised by a significant amount, we would expect the new monetary committee at the Bank of England to raise base rates to 7-1/4 percent by the end of the year in order to take the sting out of forthcoming windfall payments and slow the pace of consumer spending."
Official interest rates are now 6.5 percent. UBS said its current forecast is for end-of-year base rates of 6.75 percent.
Cates said an aggressive tightening in monetary policy would risk a further appreciation in the value of sterling, aggravating the already unbalanced nature of the economic expansion.

The UBS study said "windfall" gains from the flotation of mutually owned building societies and insurance companies were likely to be much larger than originally estimated, possibly boosting personal wealth by around 34 billion stg this year.

It estimated that much of this money would be spent, raising consumer expenditure by perhaps one percentage point. UBS estimates consumer spending growth at 4.3 percent in 1997 compared with 3.0 percent in 1996.

If Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown ruled out a tax-raising budget on the personal sector because of his election promise not to raise income tax rates, Cates said responsibility for slowing the economy down would fall on the Bank of England.

Looking at the budget options, Cates said economic logic would suggest abolishing tax relief on mortgage interest payments and a reduction in some tax reliefs to the basic rate, but politics might rule this out.
Press reports suggested there was a strong likelihood of Brown abolishing advance corporation tax (ACT) credits to tax-exempt institutions, generating four to five billion stg in revenue.

It might be too soon to introduce the two-tier capital gains tax which Labour has considered as a means of boosting long-term investment, "but the speed at which this administration is moving means we cannot rule anything out," Cates said.
Another possible change would be a minimum level of corporation tax, implying that capital allowances could only reduce tax to a certain level.
